chapter 01 Self-attention The transformer

chapter 01 · transformer — part 2 of 2

The transformer

Self-attention moves information between positions. A transformer is what you get when you alternate that with computation within a position, wrap both in residual connections, and stack the result a hundred times.

02

From one layer to an architecture

Decoder-only, 2017 — “Attention Is All You Need”.

The overview gives the shape: a residual stream that attention and MLP blocks alternately read from and write back into. This page walks that pass end to end — what happens to a token from the moment it is text to the moment a next-token distribution comes out the top.

This page assumes the attention mechanism itself. If softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V isn't yet familiar, read self-attention first — it derives every term. Step 3 below is a one-line summary of that entire document.

What the architecture was built for: seq2seq

Self-attention handles tasks where the answer has as many outputs as inputs — one label per token, one vector per position. A great many real problems aren't shaped like that:

That one requirement forces the shape of the whole architecture. A fixed-size output head cannot work, so the model must emit tokens one at a time and be able to stop — which is what the <EOS> token is for, and why generation is autoregressive. Note also the third row: speech translation goes from audio straight to text in another language, skipping transcription entirely. That's the standard approach for languages with no writing system.

Put the 2014 design next to the thing that replaced it and the family resemblance is the point:

Those three attention blocks do three different jobs, and conflating them is the most common way this figure gets misread:

BlockQ fromK, V fromJob
Encoder self-attentionencoderencoderEvery input position reads every other — no mask
Masked self-attentiondecoderdecoderOutput position i reads only ≤ i, so training can't cheat
Cross-attentiondecoderencoderEach output position reads the whole input directly

Cross-attention is the one that removed the 2014 bottleneck, and it's why the middle block has arrows arriving from the left. Mechanically it is the same operation as §01 — softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V — with the queries and the keys/values simply sourced from different stacks.

What the transformer changed, and what it kept. The 2014 original was LSTMs, and it had a crippling flaw visible in the diagram: the encoder had to compress the entire input into a single fixed-size state before the decoder saw anything. Everything the decoder could ever know about the input had to fit through one vector.

The transformer kept the encoder/decoder split and threw out both limitations. Recurrence became self-attention — so the encoder is parallel. And the single bottleneck vector became cross-attention: the decoder issues queries against keys and values drawn from every encoder position, so it can look directly at any part of the input at any point in generation. Same three-matrix mechanism as §01, with Q from the decoder and K, V from the encoder.

One more turn of the wheel: today's LLMs are decoder-only. They dropped the encoder entirely and simply condition on the prompt as a prefix, which is why the steps below describe a single stack rather than two.

The encoder, and the block it repeats

Take the left stack on its own. The encoder's contract is simple: a sequence of vectors in, the same number of vectors out, each one now informed by the rest.

Zoom in one more level and the N× box turns out to be the same small thing repeated:

The two halves have a strict division of labour, and it explains the parameter count. Attention is the only place information crosses between positions — the feed-forward half never sees another token. So a block does one round of "look around", then one round of "think about what I found". Stack that N times and the model can chain relations: layer 1 resolves a pronoun, layer 8 uses that resolution to pick a verb sense.

Yet roughly two-thirds of all parameters live in the feed-forward half, not in attention — its inner width is about 4 × d_model. Attention gets the attention, but most of the model's capacity is the per-position MLP, which is where factual knowledge is stored.

One label on the architecture figure is still doing undeclared work. Add & Norm appears four times and is never expanded — here is what's inside it:

The residual is what makes depth possible. Because each sublayer adds to the stream instead of overwriting it, gradients reach early layers through an unbroken identity path, and a block that has learned nothing useful can output ≈0 and be harmlessly skipped. Remove the additions and a hundred-layer stack simply will not train.

Read the formula carefully — Layer Norm is not Batch Norm. The mean m and standard deviation σ are computed across the features of one vector — the x₁…x_K of a single token at a single position. Not across the batch, and not across the sequence. That independence is exactly what a transformer needs: it works with batch size 1, it works with variable-length sequences, and each position normalizes without waiting on any other, preserving the parallelism from §01.

Two updates since 2017. Most current models use RMSNorm, which drops the mean-subtraction and only divides by the root-mean-square — cheaper, and no worse. And the ordering flipped: the original normalizes after the residual (post-norm), which needs careful learning-rate warm-up to stay stable, so essentially everything since moved the norm before the sublayer (pre-norm). The figure above is the 2017 arrangement, not today's.

One last observation, and it's the reason this half of the architecture deserved its own section: the encoder is useful on its own.

One architecture, three families — and the difference is the mask, not the blocks. This is the same point §01 closed on, now at the level of whole models:

  • Encoder-only (BERT) — no causal mask, so every token sees the whole sentence in both directions. Trained by masking words and predicting them. Superb at understanding — classification, tagging, retrieval embeddings — and structurally incapable of generating, since it has no notion of "next".
  • Decoder-only (GPT, and every LLM in §2 of the overview) — causal mask, trained on next-token prediction. Generates by construction, and turned out to absorb scale better than anything else.
  • Encoder-decoder (the original transformer, T5) — both stacks plus cross-attention. Still the natural fit when input and output are genuinely different sequences, as in translation.

The blocks are identical in all three. Everything that distinguishes them is what may attend to what, and what the model is asked to predict.

The decoder: how a sequence gets produced

The encoder's job was easy to state — n vectors in, n vectors out. The decoder's job is harder, because it has to invent a sequence whose length nobody told it.

Start with a single step. The decoder needs something to begin from, so it's given a special token that means "start speaking":

Then the loop closes — the token just produced becomes the next input:

That struck-through character is a real and named problem: exposure bias. During training the decoder is fed the correct prefix at every step — the ground-truth sequence, shifted right, which is why the architecture figure labels its input Outputs (shifted right). It is never asked to continue from its own mistakes. At inference it gets nothing but its own output, so a single early error puts it in a state it was never trained on, and errors compound.

This is the origin of a whole family of fixes — scheduled sampling, beam search, and in modern LLMs the reinforcement-learning stages of §2, which train on the model's own generated trajectories rather than on curated prefixes. It is also why a model that starts an answer badly often keeps going badly rather than recovering.

Now the architecture. Cover the block that talks to the encoder and look at the rest:

Put the two stacks side by side and the resemblance is nearly total:

So what does that one word change?

Why bother masking at all, if the future genuinely isn't there? Because at training time it is. The whole target sequence is available, and the decoder processes every position in parallel — that's the efficiency from §01 that made transformers trainable at scale. Without a mask, position 2 would simply read the answer at position 3 and the model would learn nothing. The mask is what lets you keep the parallelism and still train an honest left-to-right generator: one forward pass teaches every position at once, and no position can cheat.

One thing is still missing, and it's the requirement the whole architecture was built around:

Those two special tokens are more load-bearing than they look, and you meet them constantly. BEGIN and END are what modern code calls BOS and EOS. EOS is why a chatbot's reply ends instead of running until it hits the token limit — and a model that fails to emit it is a model that rambles. It is also the exit condition one layer up: in the agent loop, "the model returned no tool call and stopped" bottoms out in exactly this token.

Which means the decoder you have just assembled is a language model. Delete the encoder and the cross-attention block, feed the prompt in as the prefix, and what remains — masked self-attention, feed-forward, residuals, linear, softmax, sample, repeat until EOS — is GPT.

Cross-attention: the block we covered up

Two sections ago the decoder was introduced with an instruction to ignore the block that talks to the encoder. Time to uncover it — it's the only piece of the architecture still unexplained, and it's the piece that joins the two halves.

Unrolled, it is the computation from §01 with one substitution:

And because those weights are a distribution over input positions, you can simply plot them:

Don't miss the note on that slide: "This is not transformer." It's a historical correction worth internalizing. Cross-attention came first — Bahdanau et al. introduced it in 2014 to fix the RNN seq2seq bottleneck from the top of this page, and Listen, Attend and Spell is an RNN model too. For three years attention was a helpful attachment to a recurrent network.

Which is what the 2017 title actually claims. Attention Is All You Need is not "attention is useful" — it is "you can delete the RNN and keep only the attachment." Everything in this document is the consequence of that deletion.

Training: how the whole thing gets fitted

Teacher forcing is what makes the mask pay off. Because the entire target is known up front, every decoder position can be computed in one parallel forward pass — and the causal mask is what stops each position from reading the answer sitting next to it. Mask plus teacher forcing is the whole training recipe: one pass supervises every position, and no position can cheat.

The cost is the exposure bias flagged earlier: the decoder is only ever trained on correct prefixes, and never rehearses recovering from its own mistakes. The obvious fix — feed it its own outputs — would destroy the parallelism, which is why it wasn't the answer. Modern practice instead adds a later stage on the model's own generated trajectories, which is exactly what §2's RL steps are.

Tips: the parts that don't fit in the diagram

Beam search is not simply "better decoding" — and knowing when it hurts is the useful part. When the task has one correct answer, as in speech recognition or translation, searching harder for the highest-probability sequence is exactly right. When the task is open-ended — a story, a chat reply, an explanation — the highest-probability sequence is bland and repetitive, because safe words are individually likely. Beam search reliably makes creative generation worse.

That's why LLM APIs expose temperature and top-p rather than a beam width: for open-ended text you want controlled randomness, not a better maximizer. The choice of decoder is a statement about whether your task has one right answer.

That claim isn't theoretical — here is what it looks like:

The finding underneath that slide is genuinely counter-intuitive: human text is not high-probability text. People constantly choose words a language model rates as unlikely — that variation is what makes prose readable. So a decoder that maximizes likelihood doesn't approximate human writing, it produces something measurably too predictable, and degeneration is the extreme case.

That paper's fix is the parameter you already use: nucleus sampling, better known as top_p. Sample randomly, but only from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to p — keeping the surprise while cutting off the nonsense tail. Alongside temperature, it is the reason modern APIs give you knobs for randomness rather than for search width.

One more mismatch, this time between what training optimizes and what anyone actually measures:

"When you don't know how to optimize, just use RL" is the sentence that leads to modern LLMs. The structure of the problem is exactly the one that returns at scale: you have an objective you genuinely care about, it can be evaluated on a finished output, and it cannot be differentiated. Gradient descent is unavailable, so you treat the score as a reward and optimize the policy with reinforcement learning.

Swap BLEU for "a human prefers this answer" and you have RLHF. Swap it for "the unit tests pass" and you have the verifiable-reward training of §2. The 2015 trick for machine translation and the technique behind today's reasoning models are the same move applied to a better reward.

Finally, the training/inference gap flagged back in the decoder section, stated plainly and then fixed:

Notice why this needs three separate papers. For an RNN, which is sequential anyway, substituting a sampled token costs nothing. For a transformer it breaks the property the whole architecture is built on: if position 3's input depends on what the model predicted at position 2, you can no longer compute all positions in one pass. Hence "Scheduled Sampling for Transformer" and "Parallel Scheduled Sampling" — both are engineering to buy the idea back without losing parallelism.

And the modern verdict: LLMs largely don't do this. They keep teacher forcing for pretraining, where parallelism is worth more than anything, and fix exposure bias afterwards with an RL stage that trains on the model's own complete rollouts — which addresses the same problem more thoroughly, and with a reward better than "match the reference token".

The steps, in order

  1. Tokenize Text → integer IDs with byte-pair encoding. A vocabulary of ~50k–200k subwords. " agent" is probably one token; a rare gene name is four. This is why models are bad at counting letters — they never see letters.
  2. Embed + position Each ID indexes a learned vector of size d_model (4096–16384). Attention is order-blind by construction, so position must be injected — modern models use RoPE, which rotates Q and K by an angle proportional to position so the dot product depends on relative distance.
  3. Attention — the one idea Every token emits a query ("what am I looking for?"), a key ("what am I?"), and a value ("what do I contribute?"). Dot every query against every key, softmax the scores into weights, and take that weighted sum of values. It is a soft, differentiable dictionary lookup, and it's learned end-to-end.
  4. Multi-head + causal mask Run that lookup in ~32–128 independent heads in parallel, each free to specialize (one tracks syntax, one tracks the previous mention of a name, one copies literally). Mask out future positions so position i can only see ≤ i — that's what makes training on a whole document teach seq_len predictions at once.
  5. MLP / feed-forward A per-token two-layer net that expands to ~4× width and back. No token talks to another here. Roughly two-thirds of all parameters live in these layers, and they behave like key–value memories — this is where "Paris is in France" is stored. Mixture-of-Experts replaces one big MLP with many, routing each token to a few, buying capacity without buying FLOPs.
  6. Residual + normalization Each sublayer computes x = x + f(norm(x)). The addition is what makes 100-layer depth trainable; RMSNorm keeps activations from exploding. Boring, load-bearing.
  7. Unembed → logits → sample Project the final vector back to vocabulary size, softmax to probabilities, then pick a token — greedy, or with temperature / top-p to control how much you sample from the tail. Append it to the input and repeat. That autoregressive loop is the only thing the model can do.
  8. KV cache (inference only) Because of the causal mask, past tokens' keys and values never change. Cache them and each new token costs one forward pass instead of n. Every serving cost, context limit and "time to first token" number you'll ever read traces back to this cache.

The same thing unrolled, with the causal mask

Q = x @ W_q          # [n, d]  what each token is looking for
K = x @ W_k          # [n, d]  what each token advertises
V = x @ W_v          # [n, d]  what each token would hand over

S = Q @ K.T / sqrt(d)          # [n, n] pairwise relevance
S = S.masked_fill(future, -inf) # can't read the future
A = softmax(S, dim=-1)          # each row sums to 1 → a lookup distribution
out = A @ V                     # weighted pull of everyone's value

Why this matters for everything above it. Attention is a lookup over whatever is in the context window, using weights that were never trained on that specific content. So a model can absorb a new API, a new file, a new tool result at inference time with no gradient update. That capability is called in-context learning, and it is the reason prompting works, the reason RAG works, and the reason an agent loop works at all — a tool result is just more context, and the machine already knows how to condition on context.

Scale, concretely

KnobTypicalWhat it buys / costs
d_model4k – 16kWidth of the residual stream — how much a token can carry
n_layers32 – 120Depth — how many rounds of "look around, then think"
n_heads32 – 128How many independent relationships per layer
context128k – 1MAttention is O(n²) in compute and O(n) in KV memory — the binding constraint on agents
params7B – 1T+Mostly MLP weights = mostly stored knowledge

Go to the formula level

Everything above is the mental model. When you want the equations themselves — five of them, and that is the whole architecture:

StepFormulaWhat it does
ProjectQ=XWQ  K=XWK  V=XWVEach token gets three roles: what it seeks, what it offers, what it passes on
Attentionsoftmax(QKᵀ / √dk)·VQKᵀ is an n×n similarity matrix; softmax makes each row weights that sum to 1; ×V makes every output a weighted average of all tokens
Multi-headConcat(head₁…headh)·WOOne softmax averages one way; h heads learn h relations, free because d_k = d/h
FFNW₂·σ(W₁x + b₁) + b₂Per-token computation, inner width ≈ 4d — the "think" half of the alternation
BlockX ← LayerNorm(X + sublayer(X))Residual makes depth trainable; X is the stream each block reads and writes

Two details carry more weight than they look. The √dk is not cosmetic — dot products of dk random terms have variance ∝ dk, so without it the softmax saturates and gradients die. And the causal mask — setting QKᵀ to −∞ above the diagonal before the softmax — is the entire difference between BERT-style and GPT-style models.

  • The Annotated Transformer (Harvard NLP) — the one to actually read. Every equation above sits directly beside the PyTorch line implementing it. The code is the clearest specification; if you know some ML, skip straight here.
